visual_elements.description_for_gemini: TOP-RIGHT CORNER of the slide, next to the headline, a torn scrapbook clipping about 30% slide width and 22% slide height, pinned with one red push-pin at the top, tilted slightly counter-clockwise. The clipping shows a humorous illustrated MEME composited inside the rectangular shape of a torn-out piece of the United States ONE HUNDRED DOLLAR BILL — the familiar green-and-cream Federal Reserve Note background (engraved scrollwork pattern, faint blue and red security threads, the '100' numerals in the corners) is preserved as the meme's backdrop, but most of the inner bill design is removed to make room for the gag. In the LEFT-CENTER of the clipping is Benjamin Franklin's classic engraved portrait FACE from the 100 dollar bill — clearly recognizable as the same gray-haired, long-haired, slightly smirking Franklin engraving, but ALIVE and animated for the meme. Franklin's MOUTH is opened impossibly wide in a Kirby-style cartoon inhale — a huge round black cartoon void of a mouth, like a vacuum hole — sucking inward. From the RIGHT side of the clipping a swirling VORTEX of cartoon paper money flutters and stretches toward Franklin's open mouth: multiple small green dollar bills (some clearly showing '$' or '100'), bright gold coins, and motion lines all curving and funneling into the mouth, getting smaller and more stretched as they approach the throat. Subtle cartoon wind-suction lines (concentric arcs) emphasize the inhale. The style is a hybrid — Franklin himself stays in the original engraved currency-portrait line art (so he's instantly recognizable as the bill), but the cartoon mouth, money stream, and motion lines are drawn in a clean modern cartoon style with bold outlines, evoking the iconic Kirby-inhaling-everything meme without depicting Kirby himself. NO TEXT inside the clipping (no captions, no speech bubbles, no dollar amounts as words, no signatures rendered). DIRECTLY BELOW the clipping, a tiny separate torn cream note paper pinned with one red push-pin, tilted slightly clockwise, in handwritten sepia cursive: 'Money Vacuum.' Visual tilt only — no degree symbols rendered.
